method: I compared the two readings and focused on one shared idea: turning movement into something that can be recorded, divided and reorganised. I also thought about examples from digital media and considered how similar ideas could be explored through a small video experiment.
related_work: Craig Reynolds’ “Flocks, Herds and Schools” shows how complex group movement can be created from a few simple rules. Mark Paterson’s “The Birth of Motion Capture” looks at how human and animal movement was recorded and analysed through early photographic technologies. Both readings explore how movement can be translated into a system.
conclusion_future_work: This week helped me understand digital thinking in a new way. It can turn movement, behaviour and even the body into information that can be analysed and changed. I would like to explore this further by making a short video experiment using recorded mouth movements and digital editing.
results_discussion: What interested me most was that digital technology does not simply copy movement. It changes movement into another form. In Reynolds’ work, the movement of a flock is reduced to simple behavioural rules. In motion capture, continuous movement is separated into images or data so that it can be studied and reconstructed. This made me think about how the body can become editable material. For example, if I record my mouth saying one sentence, I could cut the video into smaller mouth movements and rearrange them to create a different sentence. The original movement would be real, but the final result would be constructed.This creates an interesting question about what is real and what is artificial. The body, image and movement may all come from a real person, but digital editing can produce something that never actually happened. This helped me understand digital thinking not only as using computers, but also as breaking complex things into smaller parts that can be reorganised.
title: week 2
introduction: This week made me think about how digital technology changes the way we understand movement and behaviour. I was especially interested in how real movement can be broken into images, data or simple rules.
